newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-DORTMUND, SCHALKE BRING CHEER TO TROUBLED RUHR.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DORTMUND, SCHALKE BRING CHEER TO TROUBLED RUHR.

text.p: At a time when the Ruhr Valley has precious few other reasons to celebrate, its two biggest soccer clubs are giving Germany's industrial heartland something to cheer about.

By reaching the semifinals of European club competitions, Schalke and Borussia Dortmund have brought a smile to the faces of fans among the smokestacks and the steelworks after one of the toughest months of their lives.
Miners and steelworkers downed tools and took to the streets as their already beleaguered industries faced fresh threats. The game provides a much-needed break from those harsh realities.

"For many people here, football is all they've got," said Dortmund fan Holger Liebelt as he stood outside the Westfalen Stadium with thousands of other supporters clad in the club colours of yellow and black.
"It's good to able to go to the match at the weekend and forget your everyday troubles," added Liebelt, a young clerk in an industrial firm, who comes from near Essen.

The miners marched on Bonn in early March after the government announced plans to slash subsidies to the coal industry. They secured an assurance there would be no mass layoffs, but the subsidy cuts will continue.

Like other heavy industrial areas such as Merseyside in England or Clydeside in central Scotland, the Ruhr is a region where civic identity is manifested above all by a fierce pride in supporting a local football team.

The clubs were not slow to show support for the miners. Dortmund, who face Manchester United in the European Cup semifinals next week, made 250 seats available for them at a league game with Hansa Rostock.

"We're not politicians or economists so we can't say how big the subsidies to the coal industry should be," Dortmund general manager Michael Meier said. "But we want to draw attention to what coal means to our region."
Schalke, opponents of Spanish side Tenerife in the UEFA Cup, not only made league tickets available to the miners. The squad also travelled to Berlin to take part in a protest march.
The rivalry between Dortmund and Schalke for the affections of the Ruhr Valley is fierce. But perhaps it is Schalke, more than any other club, which symbolises the spirit of the area.
A recent hit entitled "You are the Ruhr Valley!" regularly blasts out of the speakers at the club's Park Stadium and the official club song refers to its heavy industrial heritage.
Schalke is a working-class area of Gelsenkirchen, a city synonymous with the Ruhr. The club is no longer based in that part of the city but it remains well aware of its origins.

Dortmund, too, have a grand old tradition which they have not forgotten. But thanks to on-field success, the club has become one of the richest in Europe, paying huge salaries to the likes of German internationals Matthias Sammer and Andy Moeller.
Schalke, on the other hand, enjoyed their glory days before the war and have rarely had the success or glamour to match the size of their support since then.

Although the club is finally enjoying impressive league and European campaigns after years of scandal and squabbling, it can boast few big stars. Libero Olaf Thon, Germany's World Cup veteran, is probably the side's best-known player.
"We buy players who fit in with us, when it comes to mentality and character -- not stars we can't pay and who don't fit in," general manager Rudi Assauer said.
The German press have dubbed Schalke's players "the Eurofighters" for their battling UEFA Cup campaign.

When crisis erupted in the steel industry just weeks after the mining dispute, it was Dortmund which found itself centre stage again. One major company, Krupp, launched a hostile takeover bid for another, Thyssen.

The move would have cost thousands of jobs across the region. Even a less radical compromise -- which began to emerge after a public outcry -- put a plant just a short drive from the Westfalen Stadium under threat.
The club's response was clear for all 55,000 supporters at the recent home game against Borussia Moenchengladbach.
"Dortmund must remain a steel production centre!" read a huge black and yellow banner across one of the main stands.
The stadium announcer also expressed the club's solidarity with the steelworkers.
How much solidarity a multi-million-dollar business can share with the unemployed or low-paid is of course a moot point.

But regardless of whether the clubs are acting out of genuine concern or a desire for good public relations, their function in providing an escape from the current problems was undisputed among fans outside the Westfalen Stadium.

"Things are getting very serious here, what with the steel crisis and the coal crisis," said Heinz Mertens, a retired construction worker. "I think it's great people have the chance to come to the football and feel good."
"It doesn't matter if you're unemployed or not, you're always a Dortmund fan," added Ernst Meier, a retired miner who has supported the club for more than 40 years.
